description:
First incarnation of the Helping Hands robot: a mobile computer that autonomously unplugs from an ordinary wall outlet, travels on battery, and plugs into another ordinary wall outlet.

Jake's broader concept is an outdoor robot with solar panels, batteries, a Mac mini and a mounted iPad; connectivity may include Starlink (voice transcription unclear, keep optional pending confirmation). This FIRST milestone focuses on ordinary wall-outlet charging and uninterrupted battery-backed operation, not solar autonomy or every eventual robot capability.

Required user flow: robot runs/charges while connected to a normal wall outlet; autonomously disconnects its plug; remains powered without rebooting the Mac, iPad, controllers or communications; manages/stows its cable; drives to a new location; locates and reconnects to an ordinary wall outlet; confirms charging and continues operating. Consider a retractable cord, as Jake suggested, and compare it against simpler reliable cable-management alternatives. A proprietary charging dock alone does not meet the requested standard-wall-outlet milestone.

Develop a concrete engineering plan and implement the useful software/simulation/prototype work that can be verified with available hardware. Define mechanical approach to locating/grasping/inserting/removing the plug, alignment/compliance and force feedback, reach/stability, cable snag prevention and strain relief, battery/charger power path, runtime/drive budget, charging detection, recovery from missing/unreachable/occupied outlets and failed mating, and safe stop behavior. Use intact certified mains interfaces and design hands-on early testing with a de-energized outlet fixture; do not improvise exposed mains wiring or autonomously attempt live physical plugging without a validated hardware setup. Outdoor operation must distinguish weather-protected mains connections from battery-only travel; account for water/dirt and outlet access.

Prefer delete/simplify/reuse. Start with the smallest convincing demonstration of unplug → battery continuity → move → replug, and produce reviewable architecture, component candidates with sourced constraints, acceptance tests, and a staged prototype plan. Tests should cover power continuity under drive/compute load, low battery, aborted unplug, incomplete insertion, false charging detection, cable payout/retraction failures, obstruction and retry limits. Separate simulated/software proof from actual physical demonstration. No purchases or claims of completed hardware without evidence.

results.identified_issue: Key simplifications: (1) no retractable reel for M1 — robot parks at the outlet with a ~1 m captured pigtail; reel only matters if it must work while tethered, and a spring reel pulls on the plug. (2) SO-101 can't supply insertion force: STS3215 30 kg·cm stall at 12 V ≈ 12 N at 25 cm vs UL 498 withdrawal 3–15 lbf (13–67 N, cited via USPTO 9502808, not the standard itself) — so a front plug carriage (lift + roll servo + spring-floating holder + load cell + face switch) and the base wheels push/pull. (3) Online power path: wall only feeds the charger, loads always on battery via inverter (M4 Mac mini is AC-only internal PSU), so no transfer gap; EcoFlow River 3 Plus (<10 ms UPS claim) is the faster alternative and Stage 0 logger decides. Victron part specs NOT verified against datasheets. Budget numbers for iPad/inverter/base are estimates. Charging confirmed only when AC present AND battery current >1 A for 5 consecutive samples (solar/regen false positive). Simulator is a toy energy/contact model — it proves controller logic and retry limits, not physics. power_continuity_log.py detects reboot by kern.boottime change and freezes by heartbeat gap >0.5 s; verified 124 s run on this Mac (idle, 80 ms worst gap) but never across an actual unplug. No base chosen in repo; carriage mount and drive budget depend on it.
results.summary: I wrote the outlet-hop plan, built a simulator with 16 passing failure-case tests, and added a Mac logger for the first real power test.
results.detailed_description:
The plan is plans/wall_outlet_hop.md, and the app will read it aloud. It deletes three things. There's no retractable cord: the robot drives right up to the outlet and charges parked, using a short certified pigtail stowed inside its body. The SO-101 arm doesn't do the plugging, because its servos top out around 12 N at reach and plugs need 13–67 N. Instead a small spring-floating plug carriage sits on the front, and the base's wheels push and pull. And there's no power switchover: the wall only feeds the battery charger, and the Mac and iPad always run from the battery through an inverter.

sim/outlet_hop is the controller plus a simulated robot that injects faults. It has 16 passing tests: low battery, aborted unplug, incomplete insertion, dead outlet, current without mains (so solar can't fake "charging"), stow failure, obstruction and retry limits. All of that is software proof only. No hardware is built or bought. The Victron part specs and the base and iPad wattages are unverified estimates.

You can try Stage 0 now with no robot. Run the Mac mini from a battery, run python3 Scripts/power_continuity_log.py --load, pull the wall plug by hand, then run --report. It only passes with no reboot and no freeze. To go further I need three answers: which mobile base, whether Starlink is in or later, and whether to try an EcoFlow River 3 Plus first (quick, but it has a 10 ms switchover) or go straight to the no-switchover battery setup.
